strengths: The manuscript presents a clear and practically relevant idea: avoid artifacts from globally fused geometry by retaining per-frame local point clouds and learning to combine retrieved anchor renderings. The motivation is intuitive and well illustrated. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/c165c7612b6949fe953288ad534ff96c/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The system combines coverage-based retrieval, cross-anchor attention, pose-guided fusion, and explicit target-camera conditioning into a coherent pipeline. Application to both CogVideoX-5B and Wan2.2-5B suggests some backbone portability.

The reported partial-revisit results are promising: the full CogVideoX variant reaches 20.96 PSNR/0.6727 SSIM, substantially above its single-anchor variant and most baselines, while the Wan2.2 variant maintains similar consistency with somewhat better perceptual scores.

The paper compares against several relevant camera-control and memory-based methods, includes both quantitative and qualitative results, and provides useful camera-control and open-domain examples. The manuscript is generally clear and appropriately cites closely related work.
weaknesses: The evidence does not adequately support the central long-horizon claim. Quantitative consistency evaluation covers only a 49-frame target segment constructed from a 70-frame source video; the 241-frame experiments are selected qualitative contact sheets without trajectory error, revisit consistency, drift, or temporal human evaluation. Still frames are particularly limited evidence for video quality and long-term temporal stability.

A central claimed contribution—coverage-driven retrieval—has no direct ablation against random, nearest-pose, overlap-ranked, or diversity-based retrieval. Table 3 only changes K, so it cannot establish that the proposed retrieval objective is responsible for the gains. Likewise, pose-guided fusion and shared attention are supported only by individual qualitative examples rather than aggregate measurements.

The global-versus-local comparison in Table 2 is confounded: the global setting uses one rendered anchor, whereas the local setting uses multiple anchors and the full multi-anchor controller. Thus the large gap does not isolate local representation from anchor count, coverage, or controller capacity. A controlled K=1 global-versus-local experiment and matched multi-anchor global baseline are needed.

The evaluation split is underspecified. Training uses 10K videos from RealEstate10K and DL3DV, while evaluation samples 500 videos from the same datasets, but the paper never states that scenes/videos are disjoint. Moreover, selecting 49 target frames and treating the remaining 21 frames from the same 70-frame sequence as historical context can provide temporally interleaved or future observations; this is not clearly representative of online long-horizon generation. Per-dataset results and uncertainty across samples are also absent.

Baseline fairness is difficult to assess. Several methods receive anchors produced by the authors' retrieval pipeline, two unpublished implementations are reconstructed with materially different adaptation schemes, and backbone/training differences remain. There are no confidence intervals, human preference studies, or evaluation of whether PSNR/SSIM improvements reflect better camera alignment rather than memory consistency.

Reproducibility and scalability details are insufficient: the FoV-overlap threshold, visibility/coverage computation, rendering and occlusion rules, attention/controller dimensions, pose representation, and stopping tolerance are not specified. Runtime, VRAM, inference latency, and the storage growth of the per-frame memory bank are unreported, weakening the claim of scalable or arbitrarily long generation. The main text also says control is applied during the first 90% of denoising steps, whereas Appendix A says 80%, and SSIM is inconsistently formatted as percentages in Table 2 versus fractions elsewhere.

Overall, this is a plausible and potentially useful system contribution with encouraging results, but under the default Algorithms/General category the missing controlled ablations and limited long-horizon validation leave the principal scientific claims insufficiently established for acceptance in the current form.

strengths: The central idea is intuitive and relevant: retaining clean per-frame point clouds can avoid artifacts introduced by prematurely fusing imperfect geometry into one global point cloud. The coverage-based retrieval and multi-anchor controller form a coherent algorithmic contribution. Review based on the supplied manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/acc9715f99d24a6c889ee7fd8e06d584/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.
The method is evaluated with two substantial video backbones, CogVideoX-5B and Wan2.2-5B, and is compared against several recent camera-controllable and memory-augmented systems.

Table 1 reports encouraging results: the full CogVideoX model improves over its single-anchor variant from 19.01 to 20.96 PSNR and from 0.6145 to 0.6727 SSIM, while the Wan2.2 version reaches 21.04 PSNR and 0.6739 SSIM. The gains in motion smoothness and temporal flicker are also promising.

The paper is generally well organized, provides implementation and baseline-reimplementation details, and includes useful visualizations of retrieval, rendered anchors, fusion behavior, and long-horizon outputs.
weaknesses: The main quantitative protocol does not convincingly test the central long-horizon generation claim. From each 70-frame real video, 49 frames are selected as targets and the remaining 21 serve as historical memory. This appears to give the system ground-truth observations distributed across the same sequence being reconstructed, rather than evaluating causal autoregressive generation from earlier frames. It consequently avoids the accumulated errors of the proposed update-retrieve-generate loop. The genuinely iterative 241-frame experiments are qualitative and show only sparse selected frames.

The key global-versus-local ablation in Table 2 is confounded: the global condition uses one fused anchor, whereas the local condition uses multiple anchors. Its values also coincide with the K=1 and full-model results in Table 1. Thus, the large 16.31-to-20.96 PSNR gain cannot be attributed specifically to local rather than global geometry; it may arise from anchor count, coverage, or the multi-anchor architecture. A controlled comparison with equal numbers of rendered views and identical controller capacity is essential.

Coverage-driven retrieval, presented as a main contribution, is not compared against meaningful alternatives such as nearest-pose, overlap-only, random, or learned retrieval. Table 3 merely shows that supplying more anchors improves reconstruction. It neither isolates the proposed greedy coverage objective nor accounts for the additional conditioning and computation.

The multi-anchor controller is insufficiently ablated. Pose-guided fusion and joint attention are supported only by individual qualitative examples, without aggregate metrics, uncertainty, or tests against strong fusion alternatives. There is also no ablation separating target-pose conditioning from anchor conditioning, despite target-pose control being credited for the camera-control gains in Table 4.

The evaluation may contain dataset leakage: training uses 10K videos from RealEstate10K and DL3DV, and evaluation uses another 500 videos from those datasets, but the paper never states that scene/video identities are disjoint from training. This is particularly consequential for reconstruction-style PSNR and SSIM evaluation.

Baseline fairness is difficult to establish. Two major baselines are unofficial reimplementations with architectural and training changes, yet their fidelity to the original methods is not validated. Other baselines use different pretrained backbones, while the proposed Wan2.2 result benefits from a stronger backbone. No parameter, memory, latency, or training-compute comparison is reported.

The claimed scalability to arbitrarily long trajectories is unsupported. The longest displayed results contain only 241 frames, with no quantitative consistency-over-time curve, repeated-trial evaluation, or analysis of drift after generated frames are added back to memory. Because every frame contributes a point cloud, storage and retrieval costs also grow with history, but complexity and runtime are omitted.

Important methodological details needed for reproduction are missing, including the exact visibility-coverage computation, FoV-overlap thresholds, occlusion handling, stopping criterion, and pose-weight normalization. There are internal inconsistencies as well: the main text applies the controller during the first 90% of denoising steps, whereas Appendix A states 80%; the algorithm initializes retrieval with the latest memory, while the surrounding text says the first rendered frame is enforced.

The premise that local memories are clean is overstated. Their point clouds are still transformed into a shared coordinate system using estimated poses, so each rendered anchor can retain pose and depth errors. The experiments compare against one particular fused-point-cloud construction and do not show that local memories outperform robust global fusion or pose-refinement alternatives.

Results lack confidence intervals, multiple-seed analysis, and human evaluation. Table 4 does not define the units or pose-estimation procedure for rotation and translation errors and even duplicates the TrajCrafter row. The selective still images cannot establish temporal quality, 360-degree consistency, or stable dynamic-character behavior. Overall, the idea has merit, but the evidence does not yet support the paper's strongest claims.

strengths: Using the default Algorithms/General contribution type, the paper offers a clear and practically meaningful idea: replacing a noisy globally fused 3D memory with independently maintained local point-cloud memories, then learning to reconcile them during generation. The coverage-based retrieval and multi-anchor controller form a coherent solution to a well-motivated failure mode of prior spatial-memory systems.

The empirical results are strong. On the 500-video partial-revisit evaluation, AnchorWeave achieves the best reported aggregate PSNR/SSIM and overall VBench quality, with improvements reproduced using both CogVideoX-5B and Wan2.2-5B backbones. The single-anchor variant is also competitive, suggesting that gains are not solely due to supplying more anchors.

The comparison set is broad and includes single-anchor camera-control methods, implicit multi-view conditioning, and global-memory methods. Providing the single-anchor variant and reimplementing unavailable memory baselines on the same backbone and training data are useful efforts toward fair comparison.

The experiments support several aspects of the design: local memory substantially outperforms the global-memory variant, performance improves monotonically with additional retrieved anchors, and the qualitative analyses illustrate how pose-aware fusion and shared cross-anchor attention can suppress conflicting geometry. Camera-control errors and extensive free-form examples add further evidence.

The paper is well organized and visually polished. The motivation, retrieval pipeline, controller architecture, and update-retrieve-generate loop are easy to follow, while the appendix supplies training details and extensive qualitative sequences.
weaknesses: The central long-horizon claim is supported mainly by selected qualitative sequences. The quantitative partial-revisit experiment generates a relatively short target segment from ground-truth historical context and therefore does not measure error accumulation when generated frames are repeatedly inserted into memory. Quantitative evaluation over multiple autoregressive segments, revisit cycles, and trajectory lengths would make the main claim substantially more convincing.

Several important ablations are not sufficiently isolated. Pose-guided fusion and shared versus separate attention receive only qualitative examples, and coverage-driven retrieval is not compared quantitatively with alternatives such as nearest-pose, overlap ranking, or random retrieval. The global-versus-local comparison also changes from one global anchor to multiple local anchors, confounding memory representation with anchor count; a one-global versus one-local and matched-coverage comparison is needed.

Evaluation reporting could be more rigorous. Table 1 appears to aggregate RealEstate10K and DL3DV rather than reporting each dataset separately, no uncertainty or repeated-run statistics are given, and generic VBench quality plus PSNR/SSIM only partially characterize spatial world consistency. Long-term feature/geometry consistency, camera-conditioned perceptual metrics, or a blinded human study would better substantiate the perceptual claims.

Reproducibility details remain incomplete for a system whose results depend strongly on geometry and retrieval: the FoV-overlap threshold and coverage computation are not precisely specified, pose-conditioned weighting lacks a mathematical definition, and rendering, resolution, sampling, and inference-cost details are limited. There is also a concrete inconsistency: the main text applies the controller during the first 90% of denoising steps, whereas the appendix states 80%.

Scalability and failure modes are underexplored. Storing per-frame point clouds grows with sequence length, concatenated shared attention becomes more expensive with additional anchors, and the claim of arbitrarily long generation is not backed by runtime or memory analysis. The approach still relies on estimated depths and poses in a common coordinate system, so pose drift, erroneous local geometry, low-overlap views, and dynamic scenes can remain problematic; the appendix's manual character masking highlights the static-scene assumption. A candid limitations discussion and broader dynamic-scene evaluation would improve the paper.

strengths: The paper addresses an important computer-vision problem: maintaining spatial consistency during long-horizon, camera-controlled video generation. The diagnosis that globally fused point clouds accumulate pose/depth misalignment is intuitive and supported by the controlled rendering diagnostic, where quality drops from 44.93 dB with one local frame to 16.15 dB after fusing 45 frames.

As an Algorithms/General contribution, AnchorWeave presents a coherent design combining per-frame local geometric memories, coverage-driven retrieval, joint cross-anchor attention, and pose-guided fusion. Replacing irreversible global fusion with independently stored local evidence is a sensible and potentially reusable design principle.

The empirical scope is reasonably broad: two 5B diffusion backbones, comparisons with several camera-control and memory-based methods, a 500-video partial-revisit evaluation, efficiency measurements, qualitative free-form trajectories, and an explore-and-revisit stress test extending to 2400 frames.

The reported results are promising. Multi-anchor CogVideoX improves from 19.01/0.6145 to 20.96/0.6727 PSNR/SSIM over its single-anchor variant, and local conditioning substantially outperforms the reported global-memory configuration. Results also transfer to the Wan2.2 backbone.

The paper is clearly motivated and generally well presented, with useful process visualizations, cost-quality measurements, and candid discussion of pose drift, reflective surfaces, error accumulation, and the static-scene assumption.
weaknesses: The central global-versus-local ablation is confounded: the global condition uses one rendered anchor, whereas the local condition uses multiple anchors and the proposed multi-anchor machinery. Consequently, the large improvement in Table 2 cannot be attributed specifically to local rather than globally fused geometry. A controlled comparison matching anchor count, controller capacity, retrieval, and training is needed.

Several claimed components lack quantitative ablation. Pose-guided fusion and shared attention are supported only by selected qualitative examples, and coverage-driven retrieval is not compared against nearest-pose, overlap-only, random, or oracle retrieval. Thus, the evidence does not establish how much each proposed component contributes.

The primary partial-revisit protocol is underspecified and may not faithfully test causal long-horizon generation: 49 target and 21 history frames are selected from the same 70-frame video, but their temporal ordering and permitted retrieval set are unclear. Results from RealEstate10K and DL3DV are aggregated rather than reported separately. The 2400-frame test uses only 20 initial images and measures similarity to the initial view, without ground-truth intermediate trajectories or uncertainty estimates.

Baseline fairness is difficult to assess. Some methods use released models, while Context-as-Memory and SPMem are author reimplementations trained on the paper's data and backbone; other methods differ in conditioning interfaces and backbone priors. No statistical variation or multi-seed analysis is reported. Moreover, the claim of best reconstruction performance is inaccurate: SEVA has higher PSNR (21.13) than both full AnchorWeave variants (20.96 and 21.04), while the SSIM advantage is very small.

Important implementation details are insufficiently specified for reproduction, including the precise visibility-coverage calculation, FoV threshold, stopping tolerance, pose-importance normalization and granularity, and camera-error estimation protocol/units. There is also an inconsistency: the main text applies the controller during the first 90% of denoising steps, while the appendix states 80%; Table 5 duplicates TrajCrafter.

Local memories avoid fusion artifacts but do not eliminate the shared-coordinate pose errors needed to render them into target views. The learned controller mitigates residual misalignment, yet robustness to systematically biased poses, depth noise, or alternative reconstruction systems is not evaluated.

Claims regarding dynamic and third-person environments are preliminary: foreground characters are manually masked, training uses static-scene datasets, and the evidence is qualitative. The method does not model out-of-view object-state changes, so its demonstrated scope is principally static environments. Overall, the idea and results favor acceptance slightly, but the confounded ablations and ambiguous evaluation protocol keep the evidence from being fully convincing.

strengths: The paper identifies a meaningful failure mode of globally fused 3D memories: pose and depth errors can accumulate into ghosted geometry that subsequently contaminates video generation. Replacing this representation with independently maintained local memories is intuitive and relevant to long-horizon, camera-controlled video generation.

AnchorWeave combines complementary components—coverage-based retrieval, multi-anchor attention, pose-guided fusion, and explicit camera-pose control—into a coherent update–retrieve–generate framework.

The reported results are promising. AnchorWeave obtains strong PSNR/SSIM and VBench scores, improves as the number of anchors increases, and is demonstrated with both CogVideoX and Wan2.2 backbones. The 2400-frame stress test and runtime/memory measurements are useful additions.

The manuscript is generally clear, includes numerous qualitative examples, discusses computational cost and failure cases, and appropriately acknowledges limitations involving dynamics, reflections, pose drift, and accumulated generated errors.
weaknesses: Under the default Algorithms/General contribution type, the evidence does not adequately isolate the proposed contributions. Most importantly, the global-versus-local comparison changes both the memory representation and the number of conditioning anchors: one global anchor is compared against multiple local anchors. It therefore cannot establish that locality, rather than increased conditioning capacity or coverage, explains the large gain.

There is no quantitative ablation of the coverage-driven retrieval strategy against nearest-pose, overlap-only, random, or other retrieval alternatives. Similarly, shared attention and pose-guided fusion are supported only by selected qualitative examples. These omissions leave two of the three principal technical contributions weakly validated.

The evaluation protocol is underspecified and potentially vulnerable to leakage. Training and evaluation both draw from RealEstate10K and DL3DV, but the paper does not state that videos or scenes are disjoint, identify official splits, or report per-dataset results. The construction of the 21-frame historical context and 49-frame target set is also insufficiently described to determine whether context frames can provide unusually direct neighboring views of every target.

Baseline comparability is limited. Several methods use their released models with potentially different backbones and training data, while Context-as-Memory and SPMem are author reimplementations whose fidelity is not independently verified. Highly relevant recent local or retrieval-memory approaches such as VMem, WorldMem, Spatia, and MagicWorld are discussed or cited but not evaluated. Statistical variation and human preference evaluation are also absent.

The strongest long-horizon and open-domain claims rely largely on curated qualitative examples. The 2400-frame test uses only 20 initial images and compares only with SPMem; its PSNR-to-initial-frame measure does not assess realism, trajectory fidelity, or consistency away from the return points. Dynamic-scene support additionally requires externally masking moving objects and is not quantitatively evaluated.

Reproducibility is insufficient for the retrieval and controller designs: the coverage measure, visibility computation, field-of-view threshold, stopping tolerance, pose features, fusion equations, and precise controller architecture are not fully specified. There is also a concrete inconsistency: the main text says the controller is active for the first 90% of denoising steps, whereas the appendix says 80%. Overall, the idea and results have merit, but these central experimental and specification gaps support a slight preference for rejection.

strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/326f36d28bcd455681da7f4c2409bfd4/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} presents a clear and practically important insight: retaining clean per-frame local geometry avoids the accumulated registration errors of a fused global point cloud, while learned multi-anchor reconciliation preserves complementary spatial evidence.

The method is technically coherent. Coverage-driven retrieval, shared cross-anchor attention, pose-guided fusion, and explicit target-camera conditioning address distinct parts of the long-horizon generation problem and can be attached to different DiT backbones.

The empirical results are strong and broad. On a 500-video partial-revisit benchmark, AnchorWeave obtains the best reported reconstruction and perceptual-quality results across seven baselines. Improvements hold with both CogVideoX and Wan2.2, and the full multi-anchor model improves materially over its single-anchor counterpart. A separate 300-video experiment also reports the lowest camera rotation and translation errors.

The paper includes useful analyses beyond the headline comparison: retrieval-count trade-offs, computational costs, global-fusion degradation, history-length scaling, a 20-scene stress test extending to 2,400 frames, qualitative free-form trajectories, and explicit failure cases. The limitations concerning dynamic content, reflective surfaces, pose drift, and error accumulation are appropriately acknowledged.
weaknesses: The component evidence does not fully isolate the proposed mechanisms. The global-versus-local experiment simultaneously changes from one global anchor to multiple local anchors, so it confounds memory representation with anchor count. Pose-guided fusion and joint attention are supported mainly by selected qualitative examples, while coverage-driven retrieval is not quantitatively compared with alternatives such as nearest-pose, overlap-only, or random retrieval.

The central quantitative benchmark is a 49-frame partial-revisit task supplied with 21 ground-truth context frames. It therefore does not directly measure the paper's hardest claimed setting: long autoregressive generation in which only generated observations are written back into memory. The 2,400-frame stress test helps, but uses only 20 initial images, reports no uncertainty, and compares principally against SPMem; broader quantitative long-horizon evaluation would make the case more conclusive.

Several reproducibility details are ambiguous or inconsistent. The main text says that control is applied during the first 90% of denoising steps, whereas the appendix says 80%; chunk length is denoted by both D and C; and the FoV threshold, precise visibility/coverage computation, controller dimensions, and pose-weight normalization are underspecified. No code-release commitment or exact train/test split is stated.

The method remains computationally demanding: the reported K=4 configuration requires 39 GB and 275 seconds for an 81-frame 480×832 video, excluding the roughly 15-second retrieval/rendering stage. The storage growth of retaining per-frame point clouds is not reported. Dynamic scenes additionally require externally supplied foreground masks, so the demonstrated dynamic capability is not yet a general solution.
